\boxed{400,\ 26.0\ \text{dB}}

SNR is a power ratio. With the same waveform shape and load, power scales as the square of the peak voltage, so  
\[
\mathrm{SNR}=\left(\frac{V_{s,\mathrm{peak}}}{V_{n,\mathrm{peak}}}\right)^2=20^2=400.
\]
Then  
\[
\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}(400)=10\log_{10}(4\times10^2)=10(2+\log_{10}4)\approx10(2.60206)=26.0206\ \text{dB},
\]
which to three significant figures is $26.0\ \text{dB}$. (Equivalently, using the voltage form $20\log_{10}20$ gives the same result.)

Since power is proportional to voltage squared across the same impedance,
\[
\mathrm{SNR}=\left(\frac{V_{\text{signal,peak}}}{V_{\text{noise,peak}}}\right)^2=20^2=400.
\]
In decibels,
\[
\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}(400)=20\log_{10}(20)\approx 26.0206\ \text{dB},
\]
which to three significant figures is \(26.0\ \text{dB}\).

\boxed{\text{SNR}=400,\ \mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=26.0\ \text{dB}}

SNR is defined as the ratio of signal power to noise power. For voltages measured across the same impedance, power is proportional to \(V^2\). Given the peak signal voltage is \(20\) times the peak noise voltage:

\[
\frac{V_s}{V_n}=20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{SNR}=\frac{P_s}{P_n}=\left(\frac{V_s}{V_n}\right)^2=20^2=400.
\]

Converting to decibels:

\[
\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}(400)=10\log_{10}(2^2\cdot10^2)=10(2\log_{10}2+2)\approx10(0.60206+2)=26.0206\ \text{dB}.
\]

Rounded to three significant figures, \(\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=26.0\ \text{dB}\). (Using \(20\log_{10}(20)\) for the voltage ratio gives the same dB value.)
